title: Proposed general features of life occur in many simple-rule systems

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Proposed general features of life occur in many simple-rule systems

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Almost any general feature proposed to characterize life, including self-organization, self-reproduction and complexity, occurs even in many systems with very simple rules, so life can only be recognized by specific shared details with life on Earth.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Indeed, following the discoveries in this book I have come to the conclusion that almost any general feature that one might think of as characterizing life will actually occur even in many systems with very simple rules.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Intelligence in the Universe” (from p. 822), p. 825. Scope: definitions of life, terrestrial and extraterrestrial

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-47: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.45

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public program catalogs can demonstrate selected features such as self-reproduction in simple systems. They cannot resolve the universal definitional conclusion or show that recognition of life must depend only on terrestrial details.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate a preregistered set of proposed life criteria and simple-rule systems, formalize each criterion, and measure how often systems satisfy it. A criterion absent from broad simple-system searches would challenge the "almost any" assertion, while many positive constructions support it only for listed criteria.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Simulation analogues may omit causal and material properties of life.

Self-organization and complexity have competing definitions.

The universe of proposed features is open-ended.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.65
data adequacy: 0.3
analysis feasibility: 0.5
operationalizability: 0.35
discriminating power: 0.4

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Additive rules such as elementary rule 90 and the two-dimensional totalistic rule in the text visibly copy patterns, and simulators make that check routine. Similar exhibitions exist for pattern formation. The step from these examples to almost any proposed feature of life, and to the conclusion that only Earth-like chemical detail counts, is not a result those simulations close.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Take a stated feature, such as self-reproduction, self-organization, or high morphological complexity, and search small cellular automata for a rule that meets a formal criterion for it. Success supports the occurrence claim for that feature; the conclusion about how observers recognize life is a further question.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Self-reproduction in an additive rule is a thin case of the biological notion.

A feature can be redefined so that the simple system fails it.

Recognized as life is a human judgment.
